- Key facts: 42-year-old with continuous auditory hallucinations, irritability and restlessness for ~1 year, beginning around the time he stopped long-term cocaine use (last use 1 year ago). Many details (timing of psychosis relative to mood episodes, suicidality, family history, meds) are unknown.
- Differential: (1) Cocaine-induced psychotic disorder — cocaine can cause psychosis, but substance-induced psychosis usually occurs during intoxication/withdrawal and typically resolves within days–weeks to a few months after cessation; persistence of hallucinations for a year after last use makes this less likely. (3) Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type — would require psychotic symptoms for a period without prominent mood symptoms (≥2 weeks) and mood symptoms present for a majority of the illness; timing is unclear, so this is possible but not established. (4) Schizophrenia — requires ≥6 months of characteristic symptoms (including hallucinations) and functional decline; fits the duration, persistent auditory hallucinations, and occupational impairment. Age of onset is a bit older than typical but still compatible.
- Given the prolonged (1 year) persistence of psychotic symptoms after cessation of cocaine, the significant functional decline, and absence of clear manic episodes or evidence that psychosis occurs only during mood episodes, a primary psychotic disorder is most likely. Among primary psychoses, schizophrenia is the best single diagnosis because duration exceeds 6 months and the clinical picture is dominated by persistent auditory hallucinations and functional impairment.

[DIAGNOSIS]
Schizophrenia
